title: First Law of Thermodynamics and Thermodynamic Processes
subcategory: Thermodynamics — First Law, Isothermal, Adiabatic, Cyclic Processes

references.label: NCERT Physics Part I, Class 11 — Thermodynamics

summary: The first law of thermodynamics (a statement of energy conservation) says heat supplied to a system equals the increase in its internal energy plus the work done by it; the type of process (isothermal, adiabatic, isochoric, isobaric, cyclic) fixes which term dominates.
explanation: The first law is ΔQ = ΔU + ΔW, where ΔQ is heat supplied to the system, ΔU is the change in internal energy (a state function — depends only on initial/final states, not the path taken), and ΔW is work done BY the system. It is essentially energy conservation applied to thermal systems: energy cannot be created or destroyed, only converted between heat, internal energy, and work. In an isothermal process (constant temperature, requires a good thermal conductor and infinitely slow/quasi-static change so heat can be exchanged), ΔU = 0 for an ideal gas, so all heat supplied converts entirely into work: ΔQ = ΔW. In an adiabatic process (no heat exchange with surroundings, ΔQ = 0, requires a perfect insulator or a very fast/sudden change so there's no time for heat exchange), ΔU = −ΔW: work done by the gas comes entirely at the expense of its internal energy, so an adiabatically expanding gas always cools. In an isochoric (constant volume) process, ΔW = 0 so ΔQ = ΔU entirely; in an isobaric (constant pressure) process, both terms are generally non-zero. In a cyclic process, the system returns to its initial state, so ΔU = 0 over the full cycle, meaning total heat supplied over the cycle equals total work done by the system — the basis of heat engines. The two specific heats of a gas, Cp (constant pressure) and Cv (constant volume), differ because at constant pressure some heat must additionally do expansion work; for an ideal gas, Cp − Cv = R (Mayer's relation).
commonMisconceptions: Confusing an isothermal process (temperature constant, ΔU = 0) with an adiabatic process (no heat exchange, ΔQ = 0) — students often mix up which quantity is held at zero.

Thinking internal energy depends on the path taken between two states — it is a state function, so ΔU is the same regardless of the process connecting the same initial and final states; heat and work, however, ARE path-dependent.
Assuming Cp = Cv for a gas — they always differ (Cp > Cv) because heating at constant pressure requires extra energy to do expansion work, which constant-volume heating does not.
examples: A gas expanding adiabatically (rapid expansion, no time for heat exchange) cools down noticeably, as seen when compressed gas from an aerosol can feels cold on release.
A Carnot engine's cycle alternates isothermal and adiabatic steps, returning the gas to its starting state each cycle (ΔU = 0 overall).
genZNote: First law of thermodynamics: energy's not disappearing, it's just switching lanes between heat, work, and internal energy.
